nameStory: The American rubyspot gets its name from the brilliant ruby-red coloration on the male's head and thorax that gleams like a precious gem in sunlight. This lustrous red "spot" makes males unmistakable as they flutter near streams and rivers, earning them their jewel-inspired common name.
description: The American rubyspot is a broad-winged damselfly that brings flashes of jewel-like color to New England's waterways. Males are particularly striking with their lustrous red head and thorax paired with a brilliant green abdomen, while females display the same brilliant green abdomen but may have either green or copper-colored markings on their thorax instead of red. Like all damselflies, they hold their wings vertically along their body when at rest, distinguishing them from dragonflies. These elegant insects are typically found near flowing water where they hunt small flying insects.

idTips.label: Male's Ruby Head and Thorax
idTips.description: Males sport a lustrous, metallic red head and thorax that catches sunlight like polished copper or a ruby gemstone - this brilliant coloration is unmistakable

idTips.label: Brilliant Green Abdomen
idTips.description: Both males and females have a brilliant, metallic green abdomen that shimmers emerald in good light, creating a stunning contrast with the thorax colors

idTips.label: Female Thorax Coloring
idTips.description: Females lack the male's ruby coloration, instead showing either green or warm copper-colored markings on their thorax with a duller, less lustrous finish

idTips.label: Broad Wings Held Vertically
idTips.description: Wings are notably broader than most damselflies and fold vertically along the body at rest, with a clear, glassy appearance that may show a slight amber tint

idTips.label: Streamside Behavior
idTips.description: Often seen perched on vegetation overhanging flowing water or making short flights just above the water's surface to catch prey

habitat: American rubyspots are found along flowing streams, rivers, and creeks throughout New England, particularly favoring areas with clean, well-oxygenated water. They prefer spots with overhanging vegetation like willows, alders, or grasses where they can perch while hunting, and are most common in partially shaded areas rather than completely open waterways.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, with males establishing territories along suitable waterways. Look for the first ruby-red flashes of color near streams in May.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when mating occurs and adults are most abundant. This is the best time to observe their brilliant colors and distinctive mating wheel behavior.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall before adults die off with the first hard frosts. Late-season individuals may appear less vibrant as their colors fade with age.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity; larvae develop underwater in stream sediments and will emerge as adults the following spring.

funFact: During mating, the male American rubyspot actually acts like a tiny bouncer - he forcefully expels any sperm that the female has stored from previous partners before depositing his own, ensuring his genes have the best chance of success!
confusionNotes: Other broad-winged damselflies in New England lack the male's distinctive ruby-red head and thorax coloration. The brilliant metallic green abdomen combined with the male's lustrous red front end makes this species unmistakable - no other damselfly in our region has this specific color combination.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their name suggesting they're uniquely American, rubyspot damselflies are actually found throughout much of the Americas. The 'American' in their name simply distinguishes them from other rubyspot species found elsewhere in their range, but they're definitely a native New England species.
compareHints: The American rubyspot is the only member of its genus found in New England, making identification straightforward. Compared to other broad-winged damselflies in the region, it's distinguished by its brilliant metallic coloration - most other species in this family are much duller with browns, blacks, or muted greens rather than the rubyspot's jewel-like ruby and emerald tones.
